Weak force. One of the four fundamental interactions in physics, responsible for radioactive decay and neutrino interactions. Operating at subatomic scales with an extremely short range, it mediates the transformation of quarks and leptons, enabling neutrons to decay and fueling stellar nuclear fusion. Despite its name, at very high energies the weak force becomes comparable in strength to electromagnetism, a unification principle central to modern particle physics.

Three massive bosons mediate the weak force: the W positive, W negative, and Z bosons, each approximately eighty to ninety-one giga-electron-volts per speed-of-light-squared in mass, making them thousands of times heavier than electrons. The weak force is responsible for beta decay, the process by which a neutron converts to a proton, releasing an electron and an antineutrino. This transformation is fundamental to nuclear stability and radioactivity. The weak force operates only among leptons—electrons, muons, tau particles, and neutrinos—and hadrons made of quarks. It does not mediate interactions between photons or gluons.

A remarkable property of the weak force is that it violates parity conservation. Processes mediated by the weak force do not mirror their mirror images. This discovery came in nineteen fifty-six and earned Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen Ning Yang a Nobel Prize. The weak force has an extraordinarily short range due to the high mass of its mediator bosons. Its effects vanish beyond subatomic distances of about ten to the negative eighteen meters, which explains why it is "weak" at low energies.

The weak force combines with electromagnetism into the electroweak force at energies above approximately one hundred giga-electron-volts. This unification was predicted by Sheldon Glashow and confirmed experimentally in nineteen seventy-three through neutral-current interactions. The weak force is absolutely essential for stellar nucleosynthesis. Without it, hydrogen could not fuse into helium in stars via the proton-proton chain reaction. The universe would lack heavy elements and could not support carbon-based life.

The weak force is one of only four fundamental forces known to physics, alongside electromagnetism, the strong force, and gravity. It is the only one that violates CP, or charge-parity, symmetry. It affects only leptons and certain hadrons, making it distinctly different from the other fundamental forces in its scope and behavior.
